source: Li, Naito & Shirado (2026, ICML) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench)
finding: A 65-task hidden-profile benchmark for LLM panels exists. Panels given split information do far worse than one agent given all of it. Agents do not ask for what others may know, so they converge early on the shared evidence.
numbers: 15 frontier LLMs, 65 tasks (57 validated from 200 generated candidates, 28.5% pass rate, plus hand-made). Multi-agent accuracy 30.1% under distributed info vs 80.7% for a single agent with full info. Pre-discussion hidden-profile accuracy near zero (0.008). Best model Gemini-2.5-Pro post-discussion 0.671, gap to its full-profile score -0.310; GPT-5 variants no better than GPT-4.1-mini.
quote: agents cannot recognize or act under latent information asymmetry
limits: Tasks are synthetic and LLM-generated with a validation filter; accuracy is the 'average rule' over agent votes; most ablations use one model (GPT-4.1) on 3 tasks.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 (a hidden-profile LLM benchmark exists). Our agent should treat premature convergence on shared evidence as a real failure and add an explicit step that asks what evidence is not yet on the table.

source: Li et al. (2026) HiddenBench ablations: rounds, group size, prompts (Tables 2-4)
finding: More rounds, bigger groups and friendlier or harsher prompts do not fix pooling. Only a prompt to share all information helps, and only part way.
numbers: GPT-4.1, 3 tasks. Rounds 5/10/15/20: Ypost 0.108/0.200/0.233/0.133 (peak at 15, then falls). Group size N=3..7 improvement +0.348, +0.250, +0.064, +0.197, +0.006. Prompts: very cooperative 0.242, cooperative 0.200, conflictual 0.017, zero-shot CoT 0.222, informing asymmetry 0.367, share all information 0.467.
limits: Tiny task count (3); errors are large (s.e.m. 0.03-0.10). Group-size rows use different generated tasks.
agent_relevance: Longer or larger discussion is not a remedy. Supports a short structured exchange step rather than more rounds. Partly answers gap 9: prose instructions do not replace a structural step.

source: Li et al. (2026) HiddenBench structured dissent (Table 5)
finding: Instructed dissent has a model-dependent optimum. A little helps some models, hurts others, and no level is best for all.
numbers: Four-agent groups, 0/25/50/75/100% adversarial agents. GPT-4.1: 0.233 -> 0.492 at 25%, then worse. GPT-5-mini: 0.000 at 0% (collapse), peaks 0.556-0.583 at 50-100%. GPT-4.1-mini: 0.333 -> 0.583 rising. Gemini-2.5-Flash: best at 0% (0.889), 0.306 with one dissenter. Flash-Lite: 0.667 at 0%, 0.778 at 75%.
quote: there is no universally beneficial level of dissent
limits: Few tasks per cell, no confidence intervals; dissent was a prompted adversarial stance, not a verified-correct minority. Table layout was read from extracted text, so row labels for the two GPT-5-mini / GPT-4.1-mini rows are reconstructed.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 6: the dissent level does NOT transfer across models; it needs per-model calibration, and for a strong coordinator dissent can hurt. An always-on dissent operator is risky; make it conditional.

source: Li et al. (2026) HiddenBench bottleneck isolation and Exchange-then-Decide protocol (Tables 6-7)
finding: The failure is in surfacing information, not in reasoning over it. Forced disclosure nearly removes the gap. A cheap two-stage protocol helps across model families.
numbers: 18 tasks. Baseline vs Reveal-All: GPT-4.1 0.037 -> 0.926; Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.173 -> 0.982. Secretary (summary agent): 0.241 and 0.713. Exchange stage: 2 rounds, each agent shares 1-2 decision-relevant facts and one reason the current front-runner may be wrong, then one Decide pass (5 runs, 4 agents, 3 models; Table 7 numbers not extracted).
limits: Reveal-All is an oracle-like mechanism, not deployable. Protocol authors are the benchmark authors.
agent_relevance: The exchange step 'state one reason the front-runner may be wrong' is a concrete cheap dissent operator candidate. Inside one agent it means: list the evidence you have not used before committing.

source: Mansuri, Wang, Li, Acton, Eckardt, Patel & Kojaku (2026) Multi-agent discussion gains less when dissent is withheld
finding: A four-behaviour model predicts when discussion beats majority vote: discussion can overturn a wrong initial majority only if the rate at which agents hide dissent (withholding, c) is below a critical value set by the net correction rate and the internalisation rate. It reconciles 'debate helps' with 'debate hurts'.
numbers: Nine LLMs, three instructions (A honest, B none, C value cohesion), HiddenBench, MedEInst and MuSiQue (a fourth benchmark in the appendix). Gain from discussion falls as the margin (estimated c minus critical c) grows; clear on HiddenBench and MedEInst, unclear on MuSiQue. Reasoning models stay above threshold under all instructions because internalisation is high. Temperature 0.7.
limits: Preprint (Sept 2026); hosted models may change; mean-field idealisation; relation weak on MuSiQue.
agent_relevance: Best theory found for gaps 6, 9 and 10: agreement level is largely a prompt property (instruction C pushes teams into wrong consensus) and the key variable is whether private dissent is stated aloud. Our agent should log private answer separately from stated answer.

source: Mansuri et al. (2026) causal follow-up: fixing withholding, and turning reasoning off
finding: Forcing withholding to 100% nearly removes the discussion gain, so the link is causal. Turning reasoning off in the same model raises the gain.
numbers: Four LLMs, withholding fixed externally: c=1 nearly removed the gain; c=0 raised it only for gpt-4o-mini (the model whose public statements and private answers diverged); the other three already agreed in private and in public so had no gain to add. Reasoning off lowers internalisation and raises net correction and gain, with no consistent shift in withholding.
quote: Turning reasoning off also increases the gain
limits: Four models only; gains for strong models are near zero to begin with. 'Reasoning off helps' may be model specific.
agent_relevance: Warning against 'think harder in the dissent round': reasoning can lock in the stated majority answer. Keep an independent private commitment before any peer or critic text (gap 9, partial support).

source: Babu et al. (2026) Consilience: Conformally Calibrated Communication Control for Hidden-Profile Multi-Agent Reasoning
finding: A controller that tracks uncertainty, disagreement, evidence gain, redundancy and a premature-consensus signal and picks the next move (challenge, clarify, seek evidence, route) lifts hidden-profile accuracy a lot, sometimes above the full-information baseline.
numbers: HiddenBench-style tasks, 12 open and closed models. Best controller 0.83 average vs 0.26 for fixed round-robin; unstructured discussion 0.285; full-information reference 0.731 average; rules controller 0.843 beats it. Second benchmark (GroupTravelBench-derived): uncontrolled 0.498, best LLM+Vote 0.668; unseen-task MLP 0.73 vs all-task 0.77.
limits: Uses the Li et al. benchmark but tuned on the same task family; no token-matched single-agent baseline.
agent_relevance: A second team confirms hidden-profile failure and shows a state-tracking controller removes most of it. A premature-consensus flag as a state variable is a direct design hint.

source: Imel, Charradi, Sghir & El Khammar (2026) Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions (CrossProfile)
finding: After a group discusses, what the final decision maker is shown matters. Decision models weigh facts that many agents hold more heavily (social proof), and the full transcript can do worse than no notes.
numbers: 60 templates, 480 tasks; Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, two DeepSeek models. A perfect relevance filter loses 23-31 points to rarest-first in the classic hidden-profile layout (decoys are on topic). Removing attribution tags or shuffling them raises accuracy 13-24 points. Complete transcript gives lower accuracy than no notes in natural discussions.
limits: Small open models; synthetic templates with verified keys; preprint.
agent_relevance: A second route to premature agreement: counting how many sources said it. Our agent should strip 'N samples agree' counts when judging evidence, or judge items blind to who held them.

source: Prakash (2026) From Debate to Deliberation: Structured Collective Reasoning with Typed Epistemic Acts (DCI)
finding: Structured deliberation (typed moves, minority report, reopen conditions) beats unstructured debate and wins on hidden-profile tasks, but a single agent beats it overall and uses about 62 times fewer tokens.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash, 45 tasks, seven domains. Non-routine (n=40): DCI minus unstructured debate +0.95 (95% CI +0.41 to +1.54). Hidden-profile score 9.56 (vs debate +1.44, CI +0.57 to +2.43). Overall single agent minus DCI 0.60 (CI 0.15 to 1.06); single agent 8.84 vs DCI 8.62. Tokens: single agent 3,809 per task, DCI about 62x; quality per 1k tokens 2.320 for single agent. DCI wrote minority reports in 98% of runs.
limits: Single author, LLM-judged scores, one model, small n; components not separable.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: at token accounting the single agent wins everywhere except hidden-profile integration. An internal dissent step must cost a few percent of tokens to be worth it.

source: Wunderlich, Kaesberg, Wahle, Ruas & Gipp (2026) Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency: Pareto-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Under comparable inference budgets on MMLU-Pro, debate slightly beats self-consistency and mixture-of-agents clearly beats it. Self-consistency saturates earlier.
numbers: 34 configurations, over 100 evaluations, MMLU-Pro and BBH. MMLU-Pro best: CoT 64.3% -> MoA 71.4% (+7.1 pp), self-consistency 68.7%, debate 70.0%, at up to 20x CoT budget. Abstract says debate +1.3 and MoA +2.7 over SC at equal budget; intro text says +1.4 for debate (70.0 minus 68.7 is 1.3). Gain largest on hard tasks (+9.0 pp at 15-20x) and +2.2 pp on easy.
limits: Same lab as the Kaesberg voting paper; no dissent-specific arm; the 1.3 vs 1.4 figures are inconsistent in the paper.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: matched-budget debate is not worse than k-sample vote and is slightly better, unlike Choi et al. (2025). Still no internal-dissent-vs-vote test at equal tokens; that stays open.

source: He, Chen, Yang, Qiao, Ju, Liu, Wen & Liu (2026) Minority Sentinel: When to Overturn Majority Voting in Multi-Agent LLM Debates (full text)
finding: Full read: it is not a verifier-gated rule. It is a LightGBM classifier on debate-log features (10 dynamics, 4 voting, 8 semantic-audit features from GPT-4o) that decides when to overturn a 2:1 majority. An LLM judge doing the same job loses accuracy.
numbers: 3 heterogeneous agents, 2 rounds, 6 benchmarks. 39.1% of samples are 2:1 splits; in 25.5% of those the minority is right. Majority vote 74.3% vs oracle 84.3% (10.0 pp margin). Sentinel: 39 correct flips, 9 wrong flips, flip precision 81.2%, net gain +1.71%; 20 seeds mean +1.65% (std 0.19, min +1.31, max +2.00). LLM judge: 70 correct, 94 wrong flips, precision 42.7%, net gain -1.37%. Removing all audit features cuts net gain only 0.29 pp.
quote: an LLM judge reading debate logs and making rulings yields negative
limits: One author team, no outside replication found (SIGIR 2026 workshop paper). Only 2:1 splits with 3 agents. Per-dataset thresholds tuned on small samples. Net gain of 1.7 pp is small; GPT-4o audit cost not token-matched.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays OPEN: no non-author replication, and the rule is a trained classifier, not a verifier gate. Lesson: an LLM judge overturning the majority is net harmful (-1.37), so overturn needs a non-LLM signal such as a checker or tests.

source: Hu & Qu (2026) Most LLM Conformity Needs No Speaker: Measuring the Speaker-Free Floor in Peer-Pressure Benchmarks
finding: Most apparent conformity is not social. Repeating a wrong answer with no speaker makes models drop correct answers almost as often as an expert panel does. Source framing adds a small increment.
numbers: Six open-weight instruction-tuned models (Qwen 1.5B/3B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B), seven QA/reasoning sets. Harmful revision of initially correct answers: no-source 66.5%, plain re-ask 10.3%, strongest expert-panel framing 79.4% (+12.9 pp over no-source). Persists on off-ceiling items (77.3%) and open-ended with options hidden (75.4%), and with paraphrased assertions. Flipped models are usually confidently wrong; temperature rescaling does not recover the original answer in 42 of 42 model-by-dataset cells.
limits: Small open instruction-tuned models only (no base models), so training vs prompt cannot be separated. Not frontier.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the effect is mostly an in-context repetition effect, present without a social frame. For our agent: any repeated assertion of a wrong answer, even its own earlier sample, may already flip it. Gap 2 stays open for frontier models.

source: Hussain & Nielbo (2026) Conformity Mitigations in Large Language Models Lie on a Single Resistance-Receptivity Frontier
finding: Every conformity fix tested trades away the ability to accept correct peer answers. Only reasoning on derivable questions improves both.
numbers: 23 open-weight models (14B and up), 19 conditions, 3 datasets, over 1 million graded responses. A unanimous wrong group reverses 22.8% of correct MMLU answers, 54.8% on GPQA, 71.0% on free-form SimpleQA. Six methods lie on one frontier (R-squared 0.80-0.90). Reflection: +7.9 points MMLU resistance, -15.3 receptivity. Reasoning on self-derivable MMLU subjects: resistance +7.2, receptivity +9.6.
limits: Open-weight models only; peer script fixed and unanimous (no graded majority); wrong answers written by GPT-4o; no closed frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (partial): flip rate rises sharply when the model cannot verify the answer itself (SimpleQA 71.0%). A dissent operator that only resists will cost corrections; the agent needs a check that works on derivable answers. Measure receptivity whenever anti-conformity is added.

source: Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026) The Ringelmann Effect in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Scaling Law for Effective Team Size
finding: Dense debating agents are strongly correlated and effective team size saturates. A random-noise placebo tracks self-correction, which implies much of the debate gain is re-evaluation, not peer content.
numbers: R(N) = Neff/N = 1/(1 + c(N-1)N^-alpha), fits every condition at R-squared above 0.99. Thirty dense debating agents give no more answer diversity than one on MMLU-Hard. Self-consistency has alpha=0 so Neff=N. Only heterogeneous (different-architecture) teams lower c; communication mode and peer count do not. Qwen3-8B thinking 87.2% solo on MMLU-Hard.
limits: Fit on mostly open 7B-32B models; frontier check is a few Gemini settings; preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (indirect): independent sampling keeps full effective N while interaction collapses it, so for one agent the independence of the k samples is worth more than dissent talk. Supports sample first, interact later.

source: Bellina, De Marzo & Garcia (2026) Conformity and Social Impact on AI Agents
finding: Multimodal LLM agents show Asch-style conformity that follows Social Impact Theory: it rises with group size and unanimity and with task difficulty. Large models are less conformist on easy items but stay vulnerable at their competence boundary.
numbers: Only the abstract was read this session; no figures extracted.
limits: Abstract level only. Visual tasks, not text reasoning.
agent_relevance: Context that vulnerability moves to the edge of competence, which is where our agent often works. Not a number source.

source: Faulmueller, Kerschreiter, Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt (2010) Beyond group-level explanations for the failure of groups to solve hidden profiles: the individual preference effect revisited
finding: Hidden-profile failure is partly individual: members form a wrong preference from their own partial list before talking. Groups with full information all solved it.
numbers: Experiment 2 (N=95 students). Manifest-profile groups: 100% found the correct candidate; hidden-profile groups: 1 of 15 (7%), chi2(1,N=20)=15.56, p<.001. Hidden-profile individuals: 4 of 16 (25%); group vs individual n.s. (p=.333).
limits: Small cells; students; one job-candidate task. The 83% in its text is a pretest figure for one list, NOT the Stasser & Titus 1985 result.
agent_relevance: Human anchor with exact numbers (7% vs 100%). Failure starts at the individual level, so commit independently then pool is necessary but not sufficient.

source: Lu, Yuan & McLeod (2012) Twenty-five years of hidden profiles in group decision making: a meta-analysis, Personality and Social Psychology Review 16(1)
finding: Abstract-level numbers confirmed via a search snippet quoting the abstract: 65 studies, 101 independent effects, 3,189 groups. Hidden-profile groups were about eight times less likely to find the solution than full-information groups, and discussed about two standard deviations more common than unique information.
numbers: 65 studies, 101 effects, 3,189 groups; ratio about 8 (stated in words only; exact odds ratio and CI not seen).
limits: Full text not opened (publisher returned 403). Numbers from a search-result summary, so opened is false.
agent_relevance: Closes the count part of gap 4 at abstract level. Cite the human baseline as about eight times less likely (Lu et al. 2012).

source: Stasser & Titus (1985) Pooling of unshared information in group decision making: biased information sampling during discussion, JPSP 48, 1467-1478
finding: Citation and main finding confirmed via secondary pages only (shared information is discussed far more than unshared). The remembered 18% vs 83% choice rates were NOT found in any source opened this session.
numbers: No exact figures recovered. Faulmueller 2010 (d16) gives a modern hidden-profile solution rate of 7% instead.
limits: Original paper not accessible; Wikipedia 'Hidden profile' has no percentages and does not cite Lu 2012.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open for Stasser & Titus numbers. Do not quote 18% / 83% in the schema evidence.
